paras: The Cromer's Store election-day attack took place on November 2, 1880, when a mounted party of armed white men rode up to the polls at Cromer's Store in Newberry County, South Carolina, beat Black voters and fired into the crowd, killing Warren Williams. A coroner's jury found that Williams was killed by persons unknown, and no report of an arrest was found. Newberry papers blamed outsiders said to be from Laurens County and praised local whites for driving them off, while a Kansas Republican paper reprinted the account as proof of Southern election violence.

Cromer's Store was the polling place for Township 4 in the upper part of Newberry County. Witnesses at the inquest described a quiet election up to midday, with whites and Black voters at the box together and most votes already cast. Local white men had brought guns to the polls, Dr. R. C. Carlisle said, because they had been told there would be an attempt to take the box.

About noon a party of horsemen with sticks, clubs and pistols came down the road past Cromer's gin-house, by S. J. McCracken's later account singing "form in a row." Lewis Boyd, a sixty-year-old Black man, testified that one of them hit him twice with a stick before riding on to the well and striking others. Local white men, led by Capt. M. M. Buford, caught the riders' bridles and seemed to have stopped them, but the party wheeled and rode toward Cromer's well, where a crowd of Black men stood.

Shooting then broke out at the well, and the Black voters scattered. Milton Sanders, a Black witness, said he saw the "red shirt men" beat a colored man and then saw one of them shoot. Warren Williams fell with a bullet that, according to Dr. W. M. McCarley, entered the right side of his mouth and lodged near the base of the brain. The local whites formed a line with guns and drove the riders off; Marshal Samuel L. Atchison and Thomas F. Ray hurt their hands in the struggle, and one white man said a rock struck him on the head.

Sheriff Wheeler went to the scene with a posse, fifty men by the Columbia Register's count, and reported that peace had been restored. The same day, colored Republican voters of Township 4 signed resolutions declaring that the Democrats at the precinct were "in no wise responsible" and had done all they could to protect the attacked. On November 4 Coroner E. C. Longshore held an inquest with a jury of eleven, two of them listed as colored, which found that Williams died of a gunshot wound inflicted by some person or persons unknown.

The county chairman promised that the guilty would be punished if found, but no report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. In February 1881 the killing came up again in testimony for the Stolbrand vs. Aiken congressional contest, where the Black supervisor at Cromer's Box, Newton C. Duckett, described the attack and said 648 ballots were found in the box against 444 names on the poll list. S. J. McCracken, another Black witness, testified that about twenty-five white men beat colored men, told them to "skin out" and shot at a crowd of 100 or more.

The first report to reach print was a Columbia Register dispatch, reprinted by the National Republican in Washington on November 5 under the headline "South Carolina Methods," which called it "an unprovoked attack" by "visitors" who "were not of Newberry." The Weekly Union Times carried County Chairman M. A. Carlise's letter to the News and Courier under the heading "Murder in Newberry," stressing that local whites had driven off the "rioters" and that colored people exonerated Newberry's citizens. The Pickens Sentinel gave the killing one line among its election items.

The Newberry Herald folded the killing into an election report headlined "A Complete Triumph! White and Black Voting Together!", blamed young men "said to be from Laurens County" and called Williams "a good negro." The same issue printed the full inquest testimony, the verdict and the Black voters' resolutions. In Kansas, the Saline County Journal reprinted the Herald's paragraph with its headline as an example of Democratic papers revealing the "horrible atrocities" of Southern elections. The Herald printed the contest testimony about Cromer's Box twice, on February 16 and February 23, 1881.

Estimates of the riders' numbers ranged from eight or ten, the sworn count of two inquest witnesses, to twenty-five, twenty-five or thirty, and forty in the Columbia Register dispatch. Who fired first was also in question: Dr. Carlisle and Marshal Atchison testified that a Black man, Lewis Holman, said he had fired twice from behind the well, and Carlisle and Ray saw rocks thrown from the well, while Sanders, Boyd and McCracken described the riders beating Black men before the shooting began. The Holman statement reached the inquest only through the two white witnesses, and no witness said who shot Williams.

reader.title: Cromer's Store election-day attack
bases: A mounted party of armed white men rode up to a polling place and beat and shot at a crowd of Black voters, killing one man (A2, A3, A13); there was no accusation, seizure or custody.

The Columbia Register dispatch (A1), the county chairman's letter (A8), the Newberry Herald report (A2), the sworn inquest testimony and verdict (A3, A4) and later contest testimony (A11, A13) agree that an outside mounted party attacked voters at Cromer's and that Warren Williams was killed.

accounts.label: Columbia Register dispatch
accounts.gist: Forty mounted men 'from parts unknown' swooped down on voters, white and colored, causing a row in which one colored man was killed; an 'unprovoked attack' condemned by both parties.

accounts.label: County Democratic chairman
accounts.gist: Unknown men raised a disturbance in which one negro was killed; local whites drove off the 'rioters' and colored people exonerated the citizens of Newberry.

accounts.label: Newberry Herald
accounts.gist: Twenty-five or thirty young men said to be from Laurens charged without warning on Black voters with clubs and pistols; local whites rescued them.

accounts.label: Inquest witnesses (white)
accounts.gist: Carlisle, Atchison and Ray said eight or ten riders came up, were briefly stopped, then rode to the well where rocks were thrown and shooting began; two reported that Lewis Holman said he fired first.

accounts.label: Inquest witnesses (Black)
accounts.gist: Sanders and Boyd said the riders beat colored men with sticks before any shooting, and Sanders saw one of the riders shoot.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Williams died of a gunshot wound by some person or persons unknown.

accounts.label: Contest testimony (Black Republicans)
accounts.gist: Duckett and McCracken testified that the white party beat voters with sticks and shot at a crowd of 100 or more colored men, who fled.

framing.detail: The Columbia Register dispatch called it 'an unprovoked attack' by 'visitors' not of Newberry; the National Republican headlined it 'South Carolina Methods' with a 'White Wolves' subhead.
The Newberry Herald ran it under 'A Complete Triumph! White and Black Voting Together!', blamed Laurens outsiders, praised local whites and called Williams 'a good negro'.
The Union Times headed the chairman's letter 'Murder in Newberry', stressing that local whites drove off the 'rioters'.
The Saline County Journal reprinted the Herald paragraph as evidence of 'horrible atrocities' and bulldozing in the South.
The Pickens Sentinel gave it one line among election items.
